newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian defence minister conciliatory towards West.
newsitem.headline: Russian defence minister conciliatory towards West.

text.p: Defence Minister Igor Rodionov extended an olive branch to NATO on Tuesday, saying he was convinced the western defence alliance no longer posed a threat to Russia.
In conciliatory mood, he said a military cooperation deal could be signed with Britain before too long.

He also toned down his rhetoric on the acute problems in the Russian military -- including a cash shortage and delayed reforms -- which he previously said could have catastrophic consequences for the country.
In a briefing for journalists after meeting visiting British Defence Minister Michael Portillo, Rodionov was asked whether Portillo had persuaded him NATO was no threat.
Rodionov said yes, and added that a military cooperation deal with Britain could be signed soon.

"I am convinced. But now I have to convince millions of people, above all in Russia, and we have to work on this. Just as we have to convince the West that Russia poses no threat to the West," Rodionov said.

Portillo, who arrived on Tuesday for a two-day visit to Moscow, said both sides must work to persuade people that Russia and the West were no longer enemies. "We must each work on our public attitudes at home," he said.

Russia has vigorously opposed NATO plans to expand to the east to take in some of Moscow's former East Bloc allies, but has recently softened its stance in a tacit recognition that it can do little to stop the expansion.

"I was convinced that the British delegation...came to Russia to develop relations in the military field...searching for new ways to stabilise the situation in Europe, seeking to enhance security," he said.
"I believe that in the near future in London or Moscow it will be possible to sign a deal on military cooperation," Rodionov said. He gave no details, however.
Rodionov, who last week raised the alarm over the state of the military, told Tuesday's briefing the situation had eased.
"I wouldn't call the situation in the Russian armed forces a crisis. There are certain complications and difficulties which we, especially the government, are overcoming," he said.
"The situation a month ago was more difficult, but we have overcome it and today things are improving, including funding."
A week ago Rodionov told military top brass that Russia faced catastrophe unless it took dramatic reform measures.
"The armed forces today have come to the point where a further reduction in their combat readiness could lead to unforeseeble, tragic consequences," Rodionov had said.

Rodionov has played down talk of a military rebellion but said repeatedly that problems, which have included acute shortages in equipment and supplies and wage delays, could soon get out of control unless defence spending is increased.
Last Thursday Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin said the finance ministry had been instructed to repay 814 billion roubles ($162 million) of wages due to soldiers by November 15.
Portillo said Britain too had been through painful military reforms, including cuts in personnel like those planned by Russia, and would continue sharing its experience with Russia.

He said Britain wanted to build up cooperation in Bosnia and NATO's partnership for peace programme with former Warsaw Pact countries. He said they had also discussed the fight against terrorism and the proliferation of nuclear and chemical weapons and military reform.
